2.1.l: Pediatric Hip — Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip: Pathology & Diagnosis
2.1.b:
DDH (developmental dysplasia of the hip) is a spectrum, so first the words, then how often.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "define DDH"
- "A spectrum around a **dysplastic acetabulum**: dysplasia, instability, subluxation, dislocation."
- "Unstable at birth ≈**1%**; stays dislocated ≈**1 in 1000**."
- "No acetabular dysplasia means it is not DDH."

### Terminology
The old name told only half the story.
- The old term was **CDH** (congenital dislocation of the hip)
- Not every case is present at birth, and not every hip is dislocated
- So **DDH** replaced it in **1989** (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- "Developmental" means a process that changes with growth

### The DDH Spectrum
The acetabulum is always the primary lesion.

| Entity | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Dysplasia** | shallow socket on imaging, hip in place |
| **Instability** | hip in place but dislocatable (positive Barlow) |
| **Subluxation** | partial loss of articular contact |
| **Dislocation** | total loss of contact: reducible or irreducible |

- A dislocation with a normal socket is not DDH, for example after **septic arthritis**
- Always name the type: dislocated, subluxed, unstable, or radiological only

### Incidence
The number depends on how hard you look.
- DDH of all grades: **1 in 100 to 1 in 250** births (Handbook)
- Frank dislocation: <**1 in 1000** births
[[FIG: Fig 2.1 · 2.1
- Early ultrasound flags far more: up to **25–55 per 1000** (Campbell)
- Girls are affected ≈**5 times** more than boys
- Left hip **60%**, bilateral **20%**, right alone **20%**

#### Natural History of the Unstable Hip
- Barlow followed unstable newborn hips without treatment
- **60%** were stable by the first week
- **88%** were stable by the second month
- **12%** stayed dislocated, ≈1 in 1000 of all babies
[[FIG: Fig 2.2 · 2.1

MEMORY HOOK — the DDH iceberg
- Above water, 1 in 1000 dislocated; below it, 1 in 100 unstable; at the base, many dysplastic sockets only ultrasound sees.

### Teratologic Dislocation
This hip was out long before birth.
- Dislocated **in utero** and irreducible at birth: always **Ortolani negative**
- Seen with **arthrogryposis**, **myelomeningocele**, Larsen syndrome, sacral agenesis (Miller)
- A **pseudoacetabulum** is already present at birth
[[FIG: Fig 2.3 · 2.1
- The lecturer keeps the term DDH for the typical hip only

PITFALL — the Ortolani-negative newborn
- Two causes: severe typical DDH, or a teratologic dislocation
- Say → "**Irreducible at birth: look for a syndrome; this hip needs early surgery**"

2.2.l: Pediatric Hip — Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip: Pathology & Diagnosis
2.2.b:
DDH is multifactorial: laxity, crowding and genes meet a growing joint.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "risk factors?"
- "**F**irst-born, **F**emale, **F**amily history, **F**rank breech; plus oligohydramnios."
- "Packaging markers: **torticollis** and **metatarsus adductus**."
- "Postnatal: **swaddling** with hips adducted and extended."

### Risk Factors
Each one either loosens the hip or crowds it.

| Factor | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **First-born** | tight uterus and abdominal wall limit movement |
| **Female** | relaxin and oestrogen give more ligament laxity |
| **Breech with extended knees** | stretched hamstrings lever the head out |
| **Family history** | present in **25–33%** of cases (Handbook) |
| **Oligohydramnios**, macrosomia | less room, more compression |
| **Torticollis**, metatarsus adductus | markers of intrauterine crowding |

- First-born is the most important factor (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- Breech means **breech with knee extension**, not any breech
- A positive family history raises the risk to ≈**10%** (Campbell)
- Clubfoot has little proven link, but examine its hips anyway

PITFALL — which risk factor is strongest?
- Lecture: first-born; Miller ranks breech, family history, female, first-born
- Say → "**Breech is the strongest single factor; first-born is the commonest**"

#### When the Hip Is at Risk
- Late first trimester: an adducted hip under-builds the roof (Handbook)
- Final month: a large fetus is crowded and compressed
- After birth: laxity, then swaddling or posture

#### Why the Left Hip
- The commonest fetal position is **left occiput anterior**
- The left hip lies adducted against the maternal sacrum
- The sacrum is less forgiving than the abdominal wall

### Swaddling
A cultural habit can turn instability into dislocation.
- Legs tied straight hold the hips **adducted and extended**
- Extension stretches the hamstrings further
- A Barlow-positive hip may then dislocate completely
[[FIG: Fig 2.4 · 2.2
- Carrying the baby astride the back keeps the hips **abducted**
- Those communities have a lower incidence
- Safe swaddling must leave the hips and knees free to flex

MEMORY HOOK — the frog, not the mummy
- A baby should lie like a frog, not like a mummy: abducted, flexed hips stay home.

### Normal Hip Development
The lecture's rule: each partner shapes the other.
- The hip appears as a **cleft** in the mesenchyme at the **7th week**
[[FIG: Fig 2.5 · 2.2
- By **11 weeks** all structures are formed; then they only grow
- A normal newborn hip is deep: it cannot be dislocated
[[FIG: Fig 2.6 · 2.2
- A seated head is the best stimulus for the acetabulum
- A containing acetabulum is the best stimulus for the head

#### Role of Movement
- Joints need **active fetal movement** to shape their surfaces
- No movement: adhesions, poor synovium, attenuated ligaments
- In a cartilage model, motion alone made a ball and socket
[[FIG: Fig 2.7 · 2.2
- So DDH is expected with **arthrogryposis**, myelomeningocele, sacral agenesis

### Growth of the Acetabulum
Five growth centres build the socket; surgery can destroy them.

| Centre | What it adds |
|---|---|
| **Triradiate cartilage** | interstitial growth: depth and width |
| **Acetabular cartilage** | interstitial and appositional growth |
| **Labrum** | growth plate beneath it adds depth |
| **Secondary ossification centres** | rim growth near maturity |
| **Pelvic periosteum** | appositional growth of the flat bones |

- The triradiate cartilage is a Y of growth plates between ilium, ischium and pubis
[[FIG: Fig 2.8 · 2.2
- Beneath the articular cartilage lies thick **epiphyseal cartilage**, as in a long bone
[[FIG: Fig 2.9 · 2.2
- The labrum works like a growth plate at the rim
[[FIG: Fig 2.10 · 2.2
- Cutting it at surgery stops growth in depth

#### Secondary Ossification Centres
- **Os acetabuli** (pubis), **acetabular epiphysis** (ilium), **os marginalis** (ischium)
- They appear near maturity, after **11–12 years**
[[FIG: Fig 2.11 · 2.2
- Sepsis, labral excision or periosteal stripping damage these centres

### Growth of the Proximal Femur
The femur needs load, tone and movement as well.
- The capital femoral epiphysis ossifies at **4–7 months** (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- In infancy one physis joins head and trochanter: the **neck isthmus**
[[FIG: Fig 2.12 · 2.2
- Delayed sitting, crawling or walking deforms the proximal femur

2.3.l: Pediatric Hip — Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip: Pathology & Diagnosis
2.3.b:
Untreated, the hip changes in bone and in soft tissue; the soft tissue blocks reduction.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "obstacles to reduction?"
- "Extra-articular: **adductor longus**, **iliopsoas**, contracted **inferomedial capsule**."
- "Intra-articular: **ligamentum teres**, **transverse acetabular ligament**, **limbus**, **pulvinar**."
- "Iliopsoas over the capsule makes the **hourglass**."

### Bony Changes
Each change makes escape easier.

| Structure | Change |
|---|---|
| **Acetabulum** | shallow, steep roof → raised acetabular index |
| **Acetabulum** | more anteversion |
| **Femoral head** | small, late, flat ossific nucleus |
| **Femoral neck** | anteversion >15° and valgus (Handbook) |
| **Neck–shaft angle** | stays at the fetal 150–160° without loading |

- The dysplastic socket is shallow and not concave
[[FIG: Fig 2.13 · 2.3

### The Neolimbus
Ortolani named the ridge that fools the examiner.
- Without head pressure, acetabular cartilage grows into a ridge: the **neolimbus**
- During Ortolani the head may slide over it: a click, not a reduction
[[FIG: Fig 2.14 · 2.3
- After true reduction the head first looks low, then the ridge remodels
[[FIG: Fig 2.15 · 2.3

### Obstacles to Reduction
Learn them in two columns.

| Extra-articular | Intra-articular |
|---|---|
| Adductor longus contracture | hypertrophied **ligamentum teres** |
| **Iliopsoas** tendon | **transverse acetabular ligament** |
| Inferomedial capsule | inferomedial capsule |
| — | hypertrophied or inverted **labrum** (limbus) |
| — | **pulvinar** (fibrofatty tissue) |

#### Hourglass Capsule
- The tight iliopsoas crosses the capsule like a belt
[[FIG: Fig 2.16 · 2.3
- Upper balloon holds the head; the lower part shrinks onto the socket
[[FIG: Fig 2.17 · 2.3
- The Handbook calls it a **Chinese finger trap**
- The inferomedial capsule and transverse ligament must be opened

#### Intra-articular Blocks
- The ligamentum teres fills the socket and is excised
[[FIG: Fig 2.18 · 2.3
- Follow it at surgery: it leads to the **true acetabulum**
[[FIG: Fig 2.19 · 2.3
- The transverse ligament contracts and closes the socket mouth
- Thick pulvinar must be removed; a thin layer does not matter
[[FIG: Fig 2.20 · 2.3

PITFALL — is an inverted labrum natural?
- Handbook: inverted in frank dislocation; lecture: always iatrogenic, from repeated closed attempts
- Say → "**The natural labrum is everted; forced, repeated reductions invert it**"

#### Long-Standing High Dislocation
- Muscles and the sciatic nerve shorten with the high head
- So an older child needs femoral shortening → 03 DDH Treatment

### Growth After Reduction
A concentric reduction restarts acetabular growth.
- **Accessory ossification centres** appear in ≈**60%** after treatment (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- They look irregular, but they mean an active, growing rim
[[FIG: Fig 2.21 · 2.3
- Growth may resume for years after concentric reduction
- After about age 5, little further deepening is expected
- One hip treated by closed reduction alone became normal by 13 years
[[FIG: Fig 2.22 · 2.3
- Success needs a seated head, active movement and intact growth centres
[[FIG: Fig 2.23 · 2.3

MEMORY HOOK — the happy irregularity
- A ragged rim after reduction is the socket "under construction", not arthritis.

2.4.l: Pediatric Hip — Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip: Pathology & Diagnosis
2.4.b:
Four systems answer four questions: what type, what cause, what on ultrasound, what on X-ray.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "classify DDH"
- "Morphological: dysplasia, subluxation, dislocation; aetiological: typical or teratologic."
- "Ultrasound: **Graf** by the alpha angle; X-ray: **Tönnis** or **IHDI**."
- "Clinical phases: subluxable, dislocatable, dislocated."

### Morphological and Aetiological Types
The first label is clinical, the second is about cause.

| Type | Features |
|---|---|
| **Typical** | otherwise normal child |
| **Teratologic** | syndrome or neuromuscular disease, dislocated in utero |

### Clinical Phases
Miller's three phases follow the newborn tests.
- **Subluxable**: Barlow suggestive, a loose hip that does not leave
- **Dislocatable**: Barlow positive
- **Dislocated**: Ortolani positive early, Ortolani negative late

### Graf Ultrasound Classification
Graf measures the bony roof (alpha) and the cartilage roof (beta).
- **Alpha**: baseline along the ilium versus the bony roof line
- **Beta**: baseline versus the line along the labrum
[[FIG: Fig 2.24 · 2.4
- Bigger alpha means a deeper socket; bigger beta means a head further out
- In a normal hip the baseline bisects the head
[[FIG: Fig 2.25 · 2.4

| Graf type | Alpha | Beta | Hip |
|---|---|---|---|
| **I** | ≥60° | <55° | normal |
| **II** | 43–59° | 55–77° | dysplastic, centred |
| **III** | <43° | >77° | subluxed, labrum everted |
| **IV** | unmeasurable | unmeasurable | dislocated, labrum inverted |

- **IIa**: alpha 50–59° under 3 months, a physiologically immature hip
[[FIG: Fig 2.26 · 2.4
- The same angle is worse in an older baby
- Below **50°** (IIc), harness success falls sharply (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
[[FIG: Fig 2.27 · 2.4
- An alpha under 60° with a subluxed head is plainly abnormal
[[FIG: Fig 2.28 · 2.4

MEMORY HOOK — sixty is safe
- Alpha is the roof: **60 and over, the roof holds**; beta is the hat lifted off by a head walking out.

### Tönnis and IHDI Radiographic Classifications
Both grade how far the head has climbed out of its quadrant.

#### Tönnis Classification
- Based on the **ossific nucleus**, so it needs a visible nucleus
- Descriptive, for communication, not for planning (Prof Abdel-Ghani)

| Tönnis grade | Ossific nucleus |
|---|---|
| **1** | medial to Perkin line |
| **2** | lateral to Perkin, below the acetabular rim level |
| **3** | at the level of the superolateral rim |
| **4** | above the rim |

#### IHDI Classification
- IHDI (International Hip Dysplasia Institute) uses the metaphysis, not the nucleus
[[FIG: Fig 2.29 · 2.4
- The **H-point** is the midpoint of the top of the metaphysis
- A **45° diagonal** splits the lower outer quadrant (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 2.30 · 2.4

| IHDI grade | H-point |
|---|---|
| **I** | medial to Perkin line: normal |
| **II** | lateral to Perkin, medial to the diagonal |
| **III** | lateral to the diagonal, below Hilgenreiner |
| **IV** | above Hilgenreiner line |

PITFALL — the quadrant drawing on the slide
- The course slide labelled "Tönnis" is the IHDI drawing with its diagonal
- Say → "**IHDI works before the nucleus appears; Tönnis needs the nucleus**"

- The **H-point** is the midpoint of the top of the metaphysis
- A **45° diagonal** splits the lower outer quadrant (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 2.30 · 2.4

| IHDI grade | H-point |
|---|---|
| **I** | medial to Perkin line: normal |
| **II** | lateral to Perkin, medial to the diagonal |
| **III** | lateral to the diagonal, below Hilgenreiner |
| **IV** | above Hilgenreiner line |

PITFALL — the quadrant drawing on the slide
- The course slide labelled "Tönnis" is the IHDI drawing with its diagonal
- Say → "**IHDI works before the nucleus appears; Tönnis needs the nucleus**"

2.5.l: Pediatric Hip — Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip: Pathology & Diagnosis
2.5.b:
The signs change with age: instability in the newborn, stiffness in the infant, limp in the walker.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "signs of DDH by age"
- "Newborn: **Barlow** and **Ortolani** clunk."
- "After 3 months: **limited abduction**, **Galeazzi**, asymmetric folds."
- "Walking child: **limp**, **Trendelenburg**, waddling if bilateral."

### Examination of the Newborn
Every newborn's hips are examined, whatever the complaint.
- The baby is calm; one hip is examined at a time
- Hip and knee flexed to **90°**
- Thumb on the inner thigh, fingers over the greater trochanter
[[FIG: Fig 2.31 · 2.5

#### Barlow Test
- Adduct and push the femur **posteriorly** along its axis
- A clunk as the head leaves: a **dislocatable** hip
- Old name: the "click of exit"

#### Ortolani Test
- Abduct and lift the trochanter **anteriorly**
- A clunk as the head enters: a **dislocated, reducible** hip
[[FIG: Fig 2.32 · 2.5
- Old name: the "click of entry"
- No reduction: **Ortolani negative**, an irreducible hip
[[FIG: Fig 2.33 · 2.5

| | Barlow | Ortolani |
|---|---|---|
| Starting hip | located | dislocated |
| Manoeuvre | adduct, push back | abduct, lift forward |
| Positive means | dislocatable | dislocated, reducible |

PITFALL — click or clunk?
- A **click** is a nonspecific soft-tissue snap and means nothing (Campbell)
- Say → "**A positive test is a palpable clunk: the head translates in or out**"

#### After the First Weeks
- Test once; repeated testing is painful and may harm the hip
- After **3 months** both tests become negative as contractures form (Handbook)
- A clunk at 1–2 years may be the head sliding over the neolimbus

### Infant from 3 Months to Walking
Now the hip is stiff, and asymmetry tells the story.

#### Limited Abduction
- The most reliable sign once contractures form (Campbell)
- Abduction under **70°** in flexion is abnormal (Handbook)
[[FIG: Fig 2.34 · 2.5
- Mothers notice it at nappy changes
[[FIG: Fig 2.35 · 2.5
- Bilateral cases limit abduction symmetrically
[[FIG: Fig 2.36 · 2.5

#### Galeazzi Test
- Supine, hips and knees flexed, feet together on the couch
- The knee on the dislocated side sits lower: **femoral** shortening
[[FIG: Fig 2.37 · 2.5
- Bilateral dislocations may look level
- A congenitally short femur also gives a positive Galeazzi

#### Asymmetric Skin Folds
- Extra thigh, gluteal or labial folds on the short side
[[FIG: Fig 2.38 · 2.5
- Unreliable: normal babies have asymmetric folds too (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 2.39 · 2.5

#### Telescoping Test
- Push and pull along the flexed femur with the pelvis fixed
- Excess piston movement compared with the other side
[[FIG: Fig 2.40 · 2.5
- It stays positive after 3 months while the head is out (Handbook)

### Supratrochanteric Shortening
These older signs show a high greater trochanter.

#### Nélaton Line
- Line from the **ASIS** (anterior superior iliac spine) to the ischial tuberosity
- The trochanter tip lies on or below it normally
[[FIG: Fig 2.41 · 2.5

#### Bryant Triangle
- Vertical distance from the ASIS plane to the trochanter tip
- No normal value: compare both sides
[[FIG: Fig 2.42 · 2.5

#### Shoemaker Line and Klisic Test
- Line from the trochanter tip through the ASIS to the midline
- Both lines normally meet at or above the **umbilicus**
- Unilateral high trochanter: they meet below it, towards the sound side
- **Klisic**: a dislocated hip's line passes halfway between umbilicus and pubis
[[FIG: Fig 2.43 · 2.5

### Walking Child
Most missed hips are found when the child walks.
- Unilateral: limp, short leg, toe-walking on the short side
[[FIG: Fig 2.44 · 2.5
- A high trochanter weakens the abductors: **Trendelenburg** sign
[[FIG: Fig 2.45 · 2.5
- Walking, the trunk lurches over the weak hip
[[FIG: Fig 2.46 · 2.5
- DDH is one of four causes of a positive Trendelenburg
[[FIG: Fig 2.47 · 2.5

#### Bilateral Dislocation
- **Waddling gait** with **hyperlordosis**
- Equal leg lengths and symmetric, limited abduction
- A waddling toddler is DDH until proven otherwise, not calcium lack

| | Unilateral | Bilateral |
|---|---|---|
| Gait | limp, Trendelenburg | waddling |
| Leg length | short side | equal |
| Abduction | asymmetric | symmetric, limited |
| Spine | — | hyperlordosis |

#### Pain
- Frank dislocation is **painless**
- Dysplasia and subluxation are painful (Handbook)

### Residual Acetabular Dysplasia
The socket can fail years later, treated or not.
- Presents at ≈**11–12 years**, girls after 10
- Activity-related groin pain and abductor fatigue
- A labral tear may follow
[[FIG: Fig 2.48 · 2.5
- Standing AP and **false profile** views; MR arthrography for the labrum
- Management of the adolescent socket → 04 Pelvic Osteotomies

MEMORY HOOK — the quiet dislocation
- The fully dislocated hip is silent; the half-covered one cries: subluxation hurts, dislocation does not.

2.6.l: Pediatric Hip — Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip: Pathology & Diagnosis
2.6.b:
Screening means imaging babies with a normal clinical examination.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you screen?"
- "Every baby: clinical examination; ultrasound for risk factors (**selective**)."
- "Best timing: **6 weeks**; earlier scans over-treat."
- "A positive Barlow or Ortolani is a diagnosis, not screening: image now."

### Universal versus Selective Screening
The debate is about over-treatment.

| | Universal | Selective |
|---|---|---|
| Who | every newborn | risk factors only |
| Indications | — | breech, family history, instability |
| Drawback | many dysplastic hips that resolve | some late cases missed |
| Used in | small wealthy countries | most of the world, AAOS |

- AAOS guidance supports **no universal** ultrasound (Campbell)
- Image before 6 months with breech, family history or instability
- Egypt uses selective screening plus a national universal programme (Prof Abdel-Ghani)

### Timing
Wait for nature to fix the loose hips first.
- Ultrasound before **6 weeks** over-reads laxity
- A clinically normal baby is scanned at **6 weeks**
[[FIG: Fig 2.49 · 2.6
- An unstable hip is scanned at once to guide treatment
- Screening never replaces the Barlow and Ortolani examination

MEMORY HOOK — six weeks to settle
- Give a loose newborn hip six weeks to settle: 88 in 100 unstable hips stabilise by two months.

2.7.l: Pediatric Hip — Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip: Pathology & Diagnosis
2.7.b:
Ultrasound sees cartilage in the first months; X-ray takes over once the head ossifies.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "imaging by age"
- "Under **4–6 months**: ultrasound; after that: AP pelvis plus frog lateral."
- "Lines: **Hilgenreiner**, **Perkin**, **Shenton**; angles: **acetabular index**, CE angle."
- "Arthrogram, CT and MRI check a reduction."

### Ultrasound
It is dynamic, radiation-free and sees the cartilage head.
- Useful in the first **6 months**; useless at 1–2 years (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- Operator dependent
- Probe over the greater trochanter: the **standard coronal plane**
[[FIG: Fig 2.50 · 2.7
- That plane matches an AP radiograph
[[FIG: Fig 2.51 · 2.7

#### What to Report
- Iliac line, bony roof, labrum, capsule, femoral head
[[FIG: Fig 2.52 · 2.7
- **Alpha angle**: normal ≥**60°** (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 2.53 · 2.7
- **Head coverage**: over half outside needs treatment
- **Dynamic** stress: does the head leave?

### Plain Radiograph
X-ray becomes reliable as the nucleus appears and the soft tissues contract.
- Use it from **4–6 months**, when the head starts to ossify (Miller)
- Standard views: **AP pelvis and frog lateral**
- Never rely on one view

#### Hilgenreiner, Perkin and Shenton Lines
- **Hilgenreiner**: horizontal line through both triradiate cartilages
[[FIG: Fig 2.54 · 2.7
- **Perkin**: vertical through the lateral acetabular edge
- Their four quadrants hold a normal head **inferomedially**
[[FIG: Fig 2.55 · 2.7
- **Shenton**: neck curve continuous with the pubic ramus
[[FIG: Fig 2.56 · 2.7
- A broken Shenton line means displacement
[[FIG: Fig 2.57 · 2.7
- No triradiate visible: use the lower border of the pubic rami
[[FIG: Fig 2.58 · 2.7

#### H and D Distances
- **H**: height from the top of the metaphysis to Hilgenreiner line
- **D**: distance from the triradiate cartilage along that line
- Short H means a high head; long D means a lateral head
[[FIG: Fig 2.59 · 2.7

#### Acetabular Index
- Hilgenreiner line versus a line from triradiate to the lateral roof edge
[[FIG: Fig 2.60 · 2.7
- Larger means a shallower socket: the first number to read

| Age | Upper limit |
|---|---|
| Newborn | ≈30° (Campbell); 27.5° (Prof Abdel-Ghani) |
| 6 months | <25° |
| From 2 years | ≈20° |

- Before the nucleus shows, read the index and Shenton line
[[FIG: Fig 2.61 · 2.7

#### Centre-Edge Angle of Wiberg
- Vertical through the head centre versus a line to the lateral roof edge
[[FIG: Fig 2.62 · 2.7
- Unreliable under **5 years** (Campbell)
- After 13–14 years it should exceed **25°**
- Much more means over-coverage

#### Ossific Nucleus, Teardrop and Sourcil
- The dislocated side has a small, **late** ossific nucleus
[[FIG: Fig 2.63 · 2.7
- Absent nucleus at 1 year: suspect a missed **septic hip**
- The **teardrop** appears at 1–2 years; late appearance is a good sign after reduction
- A dense white **sourcil** means a loaded, seated head

#### Von Rosen View
- Hips abducted ≥**45°** and internally rotated
- The femoral shaft line should hit the upper acetabular edge
- In dislocation it points above, towards the ASIS
[[FIG: Fig 2.64 · 2.7
- Useful before about 2 years, even with no nucleus

#### Reading a DDH Film
This order answers "comment on this film".

| Step | Look for |
|---|---|
| Age, side | nuclei present, triradiate open |
| Position | quadrant, Shenton line, H and D |
| Socket | acetabular index raised, sourcil, teardrop |
| Head | small or late nucleus, anteversion |
| Grade | Tönnis or IHDI |

- **Coverage** is the roof over the head; **congruence** is how well they fit

- A shallow socket **raises** the acetabular index and **lowers** the CE angle

#### Pitfalls on the Film
- **Femoral anteversion** can mimic lateral displacement
[[FIG: Fig 2.65 · 2.7
- Repeat in **internal rotation** or frog lateral: the head is seated
- **Congenital femoral deficiency** shows **subtrochanteric varus**
[[FIG: Fig 2.66 · 2.7
- **Post-septic** dislocation starts with a normal socket → 08 Septic Sequelae

PITFALL — the head that only looks out
- A prominent lesser trochanter means the film was taken in external rotation
- Say → "**Never call dislocation on one AP: get the frog lateral first**"

### Arthrogram
Dye outlines what X-ray cannot see.
- Done in theatre during closed reduction, before casting
- Shows the limbus, the ligamentum teres and the capsule
[[FIG: Fig 2.67 · 2.7
- Confirms concentric reduction
[[FIG: Fig 2.68 · 2.7
- Invasive, so infection limits its use
- Medial dye pool criteria → 03 DDH Treatment

### Computed Tomography
CT checks reduction inside a spica cast.
- Axial cuts show a posterior escape through plaster
[[FIG: Fig 2.69 · 2.7
- 3D CT locates the deficient wall before osteotomy
[[FIG: Fig 2.70 · 2.7
- DDH lacks the **anterolateral** wall; cerebral palsy often the posterolateral

### Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI shows the cartilage head without radiation.
- Confirms reduction after closed reduction in a cast
- Shows labrum, limbus and obstacles in a failed reduction
[[FIG: Fig 2.71 · 2.7
- Assesses **AVN** (avascular necrosis) of the head
- Painful adolescent dysplasia: **MR arthrography** for the labrum

### Differential Diagnosis
Not every dislocated child's hip is DDH.

| Condition | Clue |
|---|---|
| **Teratologic** | syndrome, irreducible at birth |
| **Septic** | NICU stay, crying at nappy change, normal socket early |
| **Cerebral palsy** | normal hip at birth, spastic adductors |
| **Femoral deficiency** | subtrochanteric varus, short femur |
| **Anteversion** | head seated in internal rotation |

- CP with an early dislocation is DDH with CP on top (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
[[FIG: Fig 2.72 · 2.7

2.9.l: Pediatric Hip — Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip: Pathology & Diagnosis
2.9.b:
The examiner shows one picture and asks one question.

### Case 1
Boy 2 years, limp since walking: what is this film?
[[FIG: Fig 2.73 · 2.9
- Say → "Right hip dislocated: head superolateral, Shenton broken, steep roof."

### Case 2
Girl 1 year, limited abduction: comment on this hip
[[FIG: Fig 2.74 · 2.9
- Say → "Left subluxation: smaller nucleus, lateral head; IHDI II–III."

### Case 3
Girl 13 months: grade this hip
[[FIG: Fig 2.75 · 2.9
- Say → "IHDI IV left: metaphysis above Hilgenreiner; open reduction and shortening."

### Case 4
Girl 7 weeks, stiff left hip: read the two scans
[[FIG: Fig 2.76 · 2.9
- Say → "Left head out of a shallow socket: dislocated, Graf IV; an Ortolani-negative hip."
